nodes.name: Absolute logarithmic height
nodes.statement: Let \[ h:{\bar{\mathbb{Q}}}\longrightarrow[0,\infty) \] denote the absolute logarithmic height~\cite{HiSi,LangDG}.
nodes.section: Introduction

nodes.name: Lehmer's conjecture
nodes.statement: Lehmer's conjecture~\cite{Leh} asserts that there is an absolute constant $C>0$ such that if~$f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ is a monic polynomial of degree~$D\ge1$ whose roots are not roots of unity, then \begin{equation} \sum_{f(\alpha)=0} h(\alpha) \ge C. \end{equation}
nodes.section: Introduction
nodes.statement_short: There is an absolute $C>0$ with $\sum h(\alpha)\ge C$ over the roots of any monic integer polynomial whose roots are not roots of unity.
assumptions: $f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ is a monic polynomial of degree~$D\ge1$ whose roots are not roots of unity

nodes.name: Lehmer's inequality
nodes.statement: \sum_{f(\alpha)=0} h(\alpha) \ge C.
nodes.section: Introduction
nodes.label: eqn:lehmerconj

nodes.name: Dobrowolski's bound
nodes.statement: The best general result known, which is due to Dobrowolski~\cite{Dob}, says that $\sum h(\alpha)\ge C(\log\log D/\log D)^3$.
nodes.section: Introduction

nodes.name: Amoroso-Dvornicich bound for abelian extensions
nodes.statement: For example, Amoroso and Dvornicich~\cite{AmDv} show that if the roots of~$f(X)$ generate an abelian extension of~$\mathbb{Q}$, then $\sum h(\alpha)\ge D(\log5)/12$.
nodes.section: Introduction
assumptions: the roots of~$f(X)$ generate an abelian extension of~$\mathbb{Q}$

nodes.name: Borwein-Dobrowolski-Mossinghoff theorem
nodes.statement: \textup{(Borwein, Dobrowolski, Mossinghoff \cite{BoDoMo})} Let $m\ge2$, and let $f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be a monic polynomial of degree~$D$ that satisfies \begin{equation} f(X) \equiv X^D+X^{D-1}+\cdots+X^2+X+1 \pmod{m}. \end{equation} Then \[ \sum_{f(\alpha)=0} h(\alpha) \ge \frac{D}{D+1}C_m, \] where we may take \[ C_2 = \frac{1}{4}\log5 \quad\text{and}\quad C_m = \log\frac{\sqrt{m^2+1}}{2}\quad\text{for $m\ge3$.} \]
nodes.section: Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Monic integer polynomials with all coefficients $\equiv 1 \pmod m$ satisfy $\sum h(\alpha)\ge \frac{D}{D+1}C_m$ with explicit $C_m$.
assumptions: Let $m\ge2$, and let $f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be a monic polynomial of degree~$D$ that satisfies
f(X) \equiv X^D+X^{D-1}+\cdots+X^2+X+1 \pmod{m}.
nodes.label: thm:lehmodm

nodes.name: Congruence to $1+X+\cdots+X^D$ mod $m$
nodes.statement: f(X) \equiv X^D+X^{D-1}+\cdots+X^2+X+1 \pmod{m}.
nodes.section: Introduction
nodes.label: eqn:feqaop

nodes.name: Lehmer bound under a mod-$m$ cyclotomic divisibility condition
nodes.statement: For all $\epsilon>0$ there is a constant $C_\epsilon>0$ with the following property\textup: Let $f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be a monic polynomial of degree~$D$ such that \begin{equation} \text{$f(X)$ is divisible by $X^{n-1}+X^{n-2}+\cdots+X+1$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})[X]$} \end{equation} for some integers \[ m\ge2\qquad\text{and}\qquad n\ge\max\{\epsilon D,2\}. \] Suppose further that no root of~$f(X)$ is a root of unity. Then \[ \sum_{f(\alpha)=0} h(\alpha) \ge C_\epsilon\log m. \] In particular, Lehmer's conjecture~\eqref{eqn:lehmerconj} is true for this class of polynomials.
nodes.section: Introduction
nodes.statement_short: If $f$ is divisible mod $m$ by $1+X+\cdots+X^{n-1}$ with $n\ge\epsilon D$ and has no root-of-unity roots, then $\sum h(\alpha)\ge C_\epsilon\log m$.
assumptions: Let $f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be a monic polynomial of degree~$D$ such that
\text{$f(X)$ is divisible by $X^{n-1}+X^{n-2}+\cdots+X+1$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})[X]$}
m\ge2\qquad\text{and}\qquad n\ge\max\{\epsilon D,2\}.
Suppose further that no root of~$f(X)$ is a root of unity.
conclusions: In particular, Lehmer's conjecture~\eqref{eqn:lehmerconj} is true for this class of polynomials.
nodes.label: thm:intromultgp

nodes.name: Mod-$m$ divisibility condition
nodes.statement: \text{$f(X)$ is divisible by $X^{n-1}+X^{n-2}+\cdots+X+1$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})[X]$}
nodes.section: Introduction
nodes.label: eqn:fXdivXn1X1ZmZ

nodes.name: Elliptic Lehmer conjecture
nodes.statement: The elliptic analogue of Lehmer's conjecture says that if~$E/K$ is an elliptic curve defined over a number field, then there is a constant $C_{E/K}>0$ such that for all nontorsion points $Q\in E({\bar K})$ of degree $D_Q=[K(Q):K]$ we have \begin{equation} D_Q {\hat h}_E(Q) \ge C_{E/K}. \end{equation} Here~${\hat h}_E$ is the logarithmic canonical height on~$E$.
nodes.section: Introduction
nodes.statement_short: For an elliptic curve $E/K$, $D_Q\hat h_E(Q)\ge C_{E/K}>0$ for all nontorsion $Q$ of degree $D_Q$.
assumptions: $E/K$ is an elliptic curve defined over a number field
for all nontorsion points $Q\in E({\bar K})$ of degree $D_Q=[K(Q):K]$

nodes.name: Elliptic Lehmer inequality
nodes.statement: D_Q {\hat h}_E(Q) \ge C_{E/K}.
nodes.section: Introduction
nodes.label: eqn:ellipticlehmer

nodes.name: Elliptic Lehmer conjecture under an elliptic mod-$\mathfrak m$ condition
nodes.statement: Let $K/\mathbb{Q}$ be a number field and let~$E/K$ be an elliptic curve. Fix some $\epsilon>0$. Then the elliptic Lehmer conjecture~\eqref{eqn:ellipticlehmer} is true for all points~$Q\in E({\bar K})$ satisfying an elliptic mod~${\mathfrak{m}}$ condition analogous to~\eqref{eqn:fXdivXn1X1ZmZ} for some ideal~${\mathfrak{m}}$ such that ${\operatorname{\mathsf{N}}}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}{\mathfrak{m}}\ge2$ and such that~$E$ has good reduction at all primes dividing~${\mathfrak{m}}$ and for some $n\ge\max\{\epsilon{D_Q},2\}$. The lower bound in~\eqref{eqn:ellipticlehmer} will have the form $C_{E/K,\epsilon}\log m$.
nodes.section: Introduction
nodes.statement_short: The elliptic Lehmer conjecture holds, with bound $C_{E/K,\epsilon}\log m$, for points satisfying an elliptic mod-$\mathfrak m$ condition with $n\ge\epsilon D_Q$.
assumptions: Let $K/\mathbb{Q}$ be a number field and let~$E/K$ be an elliptic curve.
Fix some $\epsilon>0$.
conclusions: Then the elliptic Lehmer conjecture~\eqref{eqn:ellipticlehmer} is true for all points~$Q\in E({\bar K})$ satisfying an elliptic mod~${\mathfrak{m}}$ condition analogous to~\eqref{eqn:fXdivXn1X1ZmZ} for some ideal~${\mathfrak{m}}$ such that ${\operatorname{\mathsf{N}}}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}{\mathfrak{m}}\ge2$ and such that~$E$ has good reduction at all primes dividing~${\mathfrak{m}}$ and for some $n\ge\max\{\epsilon{D_Q},2\}$.
nodes.label: thm:mainthmintro

nodes.name: Comparison with Samuels' congruence results
nodes.statement: Our Theorem~\ref{thm:intromultgp} and some of Samuels' principal results~\cite{MR2313990} are height bounds for polynomials satisfying various sorts of congruence conditions, so we conclude this introduction by briefly describing how the results differ. Our polynomials satisfy a divisibility condition modulo~$m$, so multiplying by~$X-1$, our theorem applies to polynomials~$F(X)$ of the form \[ F(X) = (X^n-1)A(X) + mB(X)\qquad\text{for some $A,B\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$.} \] In general, we obtain a bound for all~$n$ (see Lemma~\ref{lemma:htgeelogm}), and in particular we prove Lehmer's conjecture if~$n\ge\epsilon\deg(F)$. The results in~\cite{MR2313990} apply to (factors of) polynomials that are congruent modulo~$m$ to a simpler polynomial of the same degree. For example, a typical result in~\cite{MR2313990} is a bound for (noncyclotomic factors of) polynomials~$F(X)$ of degree~$nr$ satisfying \[ F(X) = (X^n-1)^r + mB(X)\qquad\text{for some $B\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$.} \] Thus although there is some overlap, our result and the results in~\cite{MR2313990} apply to largely different classes of polynomials. It might be interesting to combine the methods of the two papers to prove a general result encompassing both.
nodes.section: Introduction
nodes.statement_short: The paper's divisibility condition covers $F=(X^n-1)A+mB$, while Samuels treats $F\equiv$ a simpler polynomial of the same degree; the classes largely differ.

nodes.name: Normalized absolute values, valuations and the absolute logarithmic height
nodes.statement: We let $M_\mathbb{Q}$ be the usual collection of absolute values on~$\mathbb{Q}$, and for any algebraic extension~$K/\mathbb{Q}$, we write~$M_K$ for the set of all extensions of these absolute values to~$K$. For~$\alpha\in{\bar{\mathbb{Q}}}$ and~$v\in M_{\bar{\mathbb{Q}}}$, we define a normalized absolute value by choosing a finite extension~$K/\mathbb{Q}$ with~$\alpha\in K$ and setting \[ \|\alpha\|_v = |\alpha|_v^{[K_v:\mathbb{Q}_v]/[K:\mathbb{Q}]}. \] We also define a normalized valuation by \[ v(\alpha) = -\log\|\alpha\|_v. \] Then the absolute logarithmic height of~$\alpha$ is defined by \[ h(\alpha) = \sum_{v\in M_K} \max\bigl\{\log\|\alpha\|_v,0\bigr\}. \] We write $M_K^0$, respectively~$M_K^\infty$, for the set of nonarchimedean, respectively archimedean, absolute values in~$M_K$.
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.statement_short: Normalizes $\|\cdot\|_v$ by local degrees, sets $v(\alpha)=-\log\|\alpha\|_v$, $h(\alpha)=\sum_v\max\{\log\|\alpha\|_v,0\}$, and names $M_K^0$, $M_K^\infty$.

nodes.name: Product formula
nodes.statement: With the above normalization we have the product formula \[ \prod_{v\in M_K} \|\alpha\|_v = 1\qquad\text{for all $\alpha\in K^*$.} \] In particular, if~$\alpha\in K$ is a nonzero algebraic integer, then \[ h(\alpha) = \sum_{v\in M_K^\infty}\max\bigl\{\log\|\alpha\|_v,0\bigr\} = \sum_{v\in M_K^0} v(\alpha). \] We also remark that \[ \prod_{v\in M_K^\infty} \|\alpha\|_v = \prod_{v\in M_K^0} \|\alpha\|_v^{-1} = {\operatorname{\mathsf{N}}}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)^{1/[K:\mathbb{Q}]}. \]
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.statement_short: Product formula; for algebraic integers the height equals the archimedean sum and the nonarchimedean valuation sum.

nodes.name: Mahler measure and heights of roots
nodes.statement: Let $f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be a monic polynomial. Then the classical Mahler measure~$M(f)$ of~$f$ is related to the heights of its roots via the formula \[ \log M(f) = \sum_{f(\alpha)=0} h(\alpha). \] In this paper we use the ``sum the heights'' notation because it has an obvious generalization to other algebraic groups such as elliptic curves. In such sums, we always include the roots of~$f$ with their multiplicities.
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.statement_short: $\log M(f)$ equals the sum of the heights of the roots of $f$, counted with multiplicity.

nodes.name: $\Phi_n(X)$
nodes.statement: For notational convenience, we let \[ \Phi_n(X) = X^n+X^{n-1}+\cdots+X+1. \] If~$n$ is prime, this is the usual cyclotomic polynomial; in general it is a product of classical cyclotomic polynomials.
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$

nodes.name: Coefficient congruence equals divisibility by $\Phi_D$ mod $m$
nodes.statement: Property~\eqref{eqn:feqaop} of Theorem~\ref{thm:lehmodm} says that all of the coefficients of the polynomial~$f$ are congruent to~$1$ modulo~$m$. This is equivalent to saying that the monic degree~$D$ polynomial~$f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ is divisible by~$\Phi_D(X)$ in the ring~$(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})[X]$.
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.statement_short: All coefficients of monic $f$ being $\equiv1 \pmod m$ is equivalent to $\Phi_D\mid f$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})[X]$.
assumptions: the monic degree~$D$ polynomial~$f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$
conclusions: This is equivalent to saying that the monic degree~$D$ polynomial~$f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ is divisible by~$\Phi_D(X)$ in the ring~$(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})[X]$.

nodes.name: Weakenings of the congruence condition
nodes.statement: Let $m,n\ge2$, and let~$f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be a monic polynomial of degree~$D$. Consider the following three conditions\textup: \begin{parts} \Part{(i)} \text{$f(X)$ is divisible by $\Phi_{n-1}(X)$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})[X]$.} \vspace{1\jot} \Part{(ii)} $m^{n-1} \mid \operatorname{Res}\bigl(f(X),\Phi_{n-1}(X)\bigr)$. \vspace{1\jot} \Part{(iii)} $\displaystyle \sum_{v\mid m} \sum_{f(\alpha)=0} v(\alpha^{n}-1) \ge (n-1)\log m$. \end{parts} Then \[ \textup{(i)} \Longrightarrow \textup{(ii)} \Longrightarrow \textup{(iii)}. \] \textup(In~\textup{(iii)}, we may work over any field in which~$f$ factors completely. The way that we have normalized our absolute values ensures that the choice of field does not matter.\textup)
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.statement_short: Divisibility by $\Phi_{n-1}$ mod $m$ implies $m^{n-1}\mid\mathrm{Res}(f,\Phi_{n-1})$, which implies $\sum_{v\mid m}\sum_\alpha v(\alpha^n-1)\ge(n-1)\log m$.
assumptions: Let $m,n\ge2$, and let~$f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be a monic polynomial of degree~$D$.
nodes.label: prop:wkmodm

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7
nodes.statement: Property~(i) says that \[ f(X) = \Phi_{n-1}(X)A(X) + mB(X) \quad\text{for some $A(X),B(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$.} \] This implies that \begin{align*} \operatorname{Res}\bigl(f(X),\Phi_{n-1}(X)\bigr) &= \operatorname{Res}\bigl(\Phi_{n-1}(X)A(X) + mB(X),\Phi_{n-1}(X)\bigr)\\ &= \operatorname{Res}\bigl(mB(X),\Phi_{n-1}(X)\bigr)\\ &= m^{n-1} \operatorname{Res}\bigl(B(X),\Phi_{n-1}(X)\bigr). \end{align*} Thus~(ii) is true. \par We next prove that~(ii) implies~(iii). For any non-archimedean absolute value~$v$ we have \begin{align} \bigl\|\operatorname{Res}\bigl(f(X),x^{n}-1\bigr)\bigr\|_v &= \bigl\|\operatorname{Res}\bigl(f(X),\Phi_{n-1}(X)\bigr)\bigr\|_v \bigl\|f(1)\bigr\|_v \notag\\* &\le \|m\|_v^{n-1}. \end{align} \par A standard formula for the resultant~\cite[Section~V.10]{lang:algebra} is \begin{equation} \operatorname{Res}\bigl(f(X),X^{n}-1\bigr) = \prod_{f(\alpha)=0} (\alpha^{n}-1). \end{equation} We take the $v$-absolute value of~\eqref{eqn:resproddef}, use~\eqref{eqn:resgemD}, and multiply over all~$v\mid m$ to obtain the estimate \begin{equation} \prod_{v\mid m} \prod_{f(\alpha)=0} \|\alpha^{n}-1\|_v \le \prod_{v\mid m} \|m\|_v^{n-1} = m^{-(n-1)}. \end{equation} Taking~$-\log(\,\cdot\,)$ gives~(iii).
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.statement_short: Resultant computation: (i) gives $m^{n-1}\mid\mathrm{Res}$; then the product formula for $\mathrm{Res}(f,X^n-1)$ over $v\mid m$ gives (iii).

nodes.name: Local bound on the resultant
nodes.statement: \bigl\|\operatorname{Res}\bigl(f(X),x^{n}-1\bigr)\bigr\|_v &= \bigl\|\operatorname{Res}\bigl(f(X),\Phi_{n-1}(X)\bigr)\bigr\|_v \bigl\|f(1)\bigr\|_v \notag\\* &\le \|m\|_v^{n-1}.
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.label: eqn:resgemD

nodes.name: Resultant as a product over roots
nodes.statement: \operatorname{Res}\bigl(f(X),X^{n}-1\bigr) = \prod_{f(\alpha)=0} (\alpha^{n}-1).
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.label: eqn:resproddef

nodes.name: Product estimate over $v\mid m$
nodes.statement: \prod_{v\mid m} \prod_{f(\alpha)=0} \|\alpha^{n}-1\|_v \le \prod_{v\mid m} \|m\|_v^{n-1} = m^{-(n-1)}.
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.label: eqnvmiDaizv

nodes.name: $\Delta(\mathcal A,m,n)$
nodes.statement: Let~${\mathcal A}\subset{\bar{\mathbb{Q}}}^*$ be a finite set of algebraic integers and let~$m$ and~$n$ be positive integers. We define \[ \Delta({\mathcal A},m,n) = \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathcal A}} \frac{1}{\log m} \sum_{v\mid m} \frac{1}{n} v(\alpha^n-1). \] The inner sum is over all $v\in M_K^0$ with $v\mid m$, where~$K$ is any number field containing~${\mathcal A}$. Our normalization of the valuations in~$M_{\bar{\mathbb{Q}}}$ implies that the sum is independent of the choice of~$K$.
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.statement_short: $\Delta(\mathcal A,m,n)$ averages $\frac1n v(\alpha^n-1)$ over $\alpha\in\mathcal A$ and $v\mid m$, normalized by $\log m$.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of $\Delta$ under powers
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal A}$ be a finite set of algebraic integers, let $j,m,n\ge1$ be rational integers, and let ${\mathcal A}^j=\{\alpha^j:\alpha\in{\mathcal A}\}$. Then \[ \Delta({\mathcal A}^j,m,n) \ge \Delta({\mathcal A},m,n). \]
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
assumptions: Let ${\mathcal A}$ be a finite set of algebraic integers, let $j,m,n\ge1$ be rational integers, and let ${\mathcal A}^j=\{\alpha^j:\alpha\in{\mathcal A}\}$.
nodes.label: prop:DAjmngeDAmn

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 8
nodes.statement: From the factorization \[ X^{jn}-1 = (X^n-1)\Phi_{j-1}(X^n), \] we see that \[ v(\alpha^{jn}-1)=v(\alpha^{n}-1)+v(\Phi_{j-1}(\alpha^n))\ge v(\alpha^{n}-1) \] for any algebraic integer~$\alpha$ and any nonarchimedean absolute value~$v$. Summing over $\alpha\in{\mathcal A}$ and $v\mid m$, and then dividing by~$n\log m$, gives the desired result.
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.statement_short: Factor $X^{jn}-1=(X^n-1)\Phi_{j-1}(X^n)$, so valuations only grow; sum over $\alpha$ and $v\mid m$.

nodes.name: Property (iii) as $\Delta(\mathcal A_f,m,n)\ge (n-1)/n$
nodes.statement: We observe that if $f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ is a monic polynomial of degree~$D$ and if we write~${\mathcal A}_f$ for the set of roots of~$f(X)$, then Property~(iii) of Proposition~\ref{prop:wkmodm} can be succintly written as \begin{equation} \Delta({\mathcal A}_f,m,n) \ge \frac{n-1}{n}. \end{equation} In particular, if $f$ satisfies the congruence \[ f(X) \equiv \Phi_D(X) \pmod{m} \] as in the statement of Theorem~\ref{thm:lehmodm}, then \[ \Delta({\mathcal A}_f,m,D+1) \ge \frac{D}{D+1}. \]
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.statement_short: Property (iii) reads $\Delta(\mathcal A_f,m,n)\ge(n-1)/n$; under the congruence of Theorem 1, $\Delta(\mathcal A_f,m,D+1)\ge D/(D+1)$.

nodes.name: Height lower bound in terms of $\Delta(\mathcal A,m,n)$
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal A}\subset\bar\mathbb{Q}$ be a finite set of algebraic integers, that does not contain any roots of unity and let~$m$ and~$n$ be positive integers. Then for all integers $J\ge1$ we have \begin{equation} \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathcal A}}h(\alpha) \ge \frac{3}{J+2}\left( \Delta({\mathcal A},m,n) \log m - \frac{|{\mathcal A}|}{n}\frac{\log(J/2+1)+1}{J}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: For algebraic integers that are not roots of unity, $\sum h(\alpha)$ is bounded below by a Fejér-weighted expression in $\Delta(\mathcal A,m,n)\log m$ and $|\mathcal A|/n$, for every $J\ge1$.
assumptions: Let ${\mathcal A}\subset\bar\mathbb{Q}$ be a finite set of algebraic integers, that does not contain any roots of unity and let~$m$ and~$n$ be positive integers.
for all integers $J\ge1$

nodes.name: Main height bound (9)
nodes.statement: \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathcal A}}h(\alpha) \ge \frac{3}{J+2}\left( \Delta({\mathcal A},m,n) \log m - \frac{|{\mathcal A}|}{n}\frac{\log(J/2+1)+1}{J}\right).

nodes.name: Choice of $J$ and the case of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: It is always possible to choose a value of~$J$ to obtain a nontrivial, i.e., positive, lower bound in~\eqref{eqn:sumhageDAmnlogm}. The optimal choice of~$J$ depends on the relative sizes of $\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n)\log m$ and $|{\mathcal A}|/n$. In the application most closely related to Theorem~\ref{thm:lehmodm}, we have \[ n=D+1\qquad\text{and}\qquad \Delta({\mathcal A},m,n)\log m = \frac{|{\mathcal A}|}{n} = \frac{D}{D+1}, \] so we get \[ \sum_{f(\alpha)=0} h(\alpha) \ge \frac{D}{D+1}\cdot\frac{3}{J+2} \cdot\left(\log m - \frac{\log(J/2+1)+1}{J}\right). \] If $m\ge5$, then we obtain a nontrivial lower bound with $J=1$, while for~$3\le m\le 4$ we need to take $J=2$, and for~$m=2$ we must take~$J=3$. Of course, the bound that we obtain is not sharp. However, our goal is not to get sharp bounds in this particular case, where other authors~\cite{BoDoMo,BoHaMo,DuMo,GaIsMoPiWi} have used intricate techniques to obtain better bounds than we could obtain even if we took more care. Instead, we aim to show how to obtain nontrivial bounds that, among other things, imply that Lehmer's conjecture is true for an interesting class of polynomials that is larger than the class considered in~\cite{BoDoMo,BoHaMo,DuMo,GaIsMoPiWi}.
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: A suitable $J$ always gives a positive bound; in the setting of Theorem 1, $J=1,2,3$ suffice for $m\ge5$, $3\le m\le4$, $m=2$.

nodes.name: Fejér kernel estimate
nodes.statement: For all $J\ge1$ we have \[ \sup_{\substack{z\in\mathbb{C}\\ |z|\le 1\\}} \sum_{j=1}^J \left(1-\frac{j}{J+1}\right)\log|1-z^j| \le \frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{J}{2}+1\right)+\frac{1}{2}. \]
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: The Fejér-weighted sum $\sum_{j\le J}(1-\frac{j}{J+1})\log|1-z^j|$ is at most $\frac12\log(J/2+1)+\frac12$ on the closed unit disk.
assumptions: For all $J\ge1$

nodes.statement: Fix $0<\epsilon\le 1$. Then Lehmer's conjecture~\eqref{eqn:lehmerconj} is true for the set of polynomials \begin{equation} \left\{ f(X)\in \mathbb{Z}[X] : \begin{tabular}{@{}l@{}} $f(X)$ is monic, its roots are not roots\\ of unity, and there exist integers $m\ge2$ \\ and $n\ge\max\{2,\epsilon\deg(f)\}$ such that\\ $\Phi_{n-1}(X)$ divides $f(X)$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})[X]$\\ \end{tabular} \right\}. \end{equation} More precisely, if~$f(X)$ is in the set~\eqref{eqn:monicmnedegf}, then \begin{equation} \sum_{f(\alpha)=0} h(\alpha) \ge \frac{\log m}{185\epsilon^{-1}\log(24\epsilon^{-1})}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Shparlinski's choice $\epsilon=\log\log m/\log m$
nodes.statement: Igor Shparlinski has pointed out that for large~$m$, we may take $\epsilon=(\log\log m)/(\log m)$ and conclude that if $\Phi_{n-1}(X)$ divides $f(X)$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})[X]$ for some $n\ge((\log\log{m})/(\log{m}))(\deg{f})$, then \[ \sum_{f(\alpha)=0} h(\alpha) \ge \frac{1}{185}+ O\left(\frac{\log\log\log m}{\log\log m}\right), \] where the big-$O$ constant is absolute.
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Taking $\epsilon=(\log\log m)/\log m$ gives $\sum h(\alpha)\ge 1/185+O(\log\log\log m/\log\log m)$.

nodes.name: Height bound from divisibility by $\Phi_{n-1}$ mod $m$
nodes.statement: Let $f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be a monic polynomial of degree~$D$ whose roots are not roots of unity, let $m,n\ge2$ be integers, and suppose that~$\Phi_{n-1}(X)$ divides $f(X)$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})[X]$. Then \[ \sum_{f(\alpha)=0}h(\alpha) \ge \begin{cases} (\log m)/264 &\text{if $\log m\ge D/16n$,} \\[1\jot] \dfrac{\log m}{(128D/n\log m)\log(16D/n\log m)} &\text{if $\log m\le D/16n$.} \\ \end{cases} \]
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: If $\Phi_{n-1}\mid f$ mod $m$, then $\sum h(\alpha)\ge(\log m)/264$ when $\log m\ge D/16n$, and a bound decaying like $(n\log m/D)/\log$ otherwise.
assumptions: Let $f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be a monic polynomial of degree~$D$ whose roots are not roots of unity, let $m,n\ge2$ be integers, and suppose that~$\Phi_{n-1}(X)$ divides $f(X)$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})[X]$.
conclusions: \sum_{f(\alpha)=0}h(\alpha) \ge \begin{cases} (\log m)/264 &\text{if $\log m\ge D/16n$,} \\[1\jot] \dfrac{\log m}{(128D/n\log m)\log(16D/n\log m)} &\text{if $\log m\le D/16n$.} \\ \end{cases}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 15
nodes.statement: Let~${\mathcal A}_f$ be the set of roots of~$f$. As noted in Remark~\ref{remark:DAfmD1geDD1}, the divisibility condition on~$f$ implies that $\Delta({\mathcal A}_f,m,n)\ge (n-1)/n$. Substituting this into~\eqref{eqn:sumhageDAmnlogm} of Theorem~\ref{thm:hageCDAmnlogm} and using~$|{\mathcal A}_f|=D$, we find that for all integers $J\ge1$ we have \begin{align*} \sum_{f(\alpha)=0}h(\alpha) &\ge \frac{3}{J+2} \left(\frac{n-1}{n}\log m - \frac{D}{n}\frac{\log(J/2+1)+1}{J}\right). \end{align*} Since we are not concerned with optimizing our constants, we observe that for $n\ge2$ and $J\ge2$, this implies that \begin{equation} \sum_{f(\alpha)=0}h(\alpha) \ge \frac{1}{J} \left(\frac{1}{2}\log m - \frac{4D}{n}\frac{\log(J)}{J}\right). \end{equation} We now consider two cases. First, if~$m$ is large, say \[ \log m \ge D/16n, \] then taking~$J=57$ gives \begin{equation} \sum_{f(\alpha)=0}h(\alpha) \ge \frac{1}{J}\left(\frac12-4\frac{\log(J)}{J}\right)\log m \ge \frac{\log m}{264}. \end{equation} Second, suppose that~$m$ is small, \[ \log m \le D/16n. \] Then we want to choose~$J$ to be an integer satisfying \begin{equation} \frac{J}{\log J} \ge \frac{16D}{n\log m}. \end{equation} In particular, since $16D/n\log m\ge256$, it suffices to take \[ J = \left\lfloor \frac{32D}{n\log m}\log\left(\frac{16D}{n\log m}\right) \right\rfloor - 1. \] Substituting~\eqref{eqn:JlogJge16dnlogm} into~\eqref{eqn:1J12m4DnlogJJ} and adjusting the constants yields \begin{equation} \sum_{f(\alpha)=0}h(\alpha) \ge \frac{\log m}{4J} \ge \frac{\log m}{(128D/n\log m)\log(16D/n\log m)}. \end{equation} Combining~\eqref{eqn:bd1} and~\eqref{eqn:bd2} completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:htgeelogm}.

nodes.statement_short: Substitute $\Delta(\mathcal A_f,m,n)\ge(n-1)/n$ into Theorem 10 and choose $J$ by cases: $J=57$ for large $m$, $J\approx\frac{32D}{n\log m}\log\frac{16D}{n\log m}$ for small $m$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 13
nodes.statement: We are given that $n\ge\max\{\epsilon D,2\}$. If $\log m\ge D/16n$, then Lemma~\ref{lemma:htgeelogm} says that \[ \sum_{f(\alpha)=0}h(\alpha) \ge \frac{\log m}{264}. \] This is stronger than~\eqref{eqn:logm185e}, since we have assumed that $\epsilon\le1$, so we are reduced to the case that~$\log m\le D/16n$. Since $n\ge\epsilon D$, this implies that \[ \frac{D}{n\log m}\le\frac{D}{\epsilon D\log m} \le \frac{1}{\epsilon\log m}, \] where the upper bound is at least~$16$. Substituting this into Lemma~\ref{lemma:htgeelogm}, we find that \[ \sum_{f(\alpha)=0}h(\alpha) \ge \frac{\log m}{(128/\epsilon\log m)\log(16/\epsilon\log m)}. \] Since~$m\ge2$, this gives something slightly stronger than the desired result.
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 15; the large-$m$ case is immediate, and in the small-$m$ case $n\ge\epsilon D$ bounds $D/(n\log m)$ by $1/(\epsilon\log m)$.

nodes.name: Amalgamated implication chain for polynomials with coefficients $\equiv 1$ mod $m$
nodes.statement: An amalgamation of Proposition~\ref{prop:wkmodm}, Remark~\ref{remark:DAfmD1geDD1}, and Theorem~\ref{thm:hageCDAmnlogm} says that if~$f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ is a monic polynomial of degree~$D$ whose roots are not roots of unity, then \begin{align*} \left(\begin{tabular}{@{}l@{}} $f(X)$ has coefficients\\ congruent to 1 modulo $m$\\ \end{tabular}\right) &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Delta({\mathcal A}_f,m,D+1) \ge \frac{D}{D+1} \\ &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sum_{f(\alpha)=0} h(\alpha) \ge \frac{D}{D+1}C_m. \end{align*}

nodes.statement_short: Coefficients $\equiv1 \pmod m$ imply $\Delta(\mathcal A_f,m,D+1)\ge D/(D+1)$, which implies $\sum h(\alpha)\ge\frac{D}{D+1}C_m$.
assumptions: $f(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ is a monic polynomial of degree~$D$ whose roots are not roots of unity

nodes.name: Canonical height and local canonical heights
nodes.statement: Let~$E/K$ be an elliptic curve defined over a number field. We write \[ {\hat h} : E({\bar K})\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \] for the absolute logarithmic canonical height~\cite[VIII~\S9]{MR2514094}, and for each~$v\in M_{\bar K}$ we let \[ \hat\lambda_v : E({\bar K}_v)\smallsetminus\{O\}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} \] be a local canonical height, normalized as described in~\cite[Chapter~VI]{ATAEC}.
nodes.section: 3 An Elliptic Analogue of $\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n)$

nodes.name: Properties of local canonical heights
nodes.statement: The local canonical height satisfies the following\textup: \begin{parts} \Part{(a)} For all $v\in M_K$ there is a constant $c(v)$ such that \[ \lambda_v(P)\ge -c(v)\quad\text{for all $P\in E({\bar K}_v)$.} \] Further, if~$v\in M_K^0$ and~$E$ has good reduction at~$v$, then we can take~$c(v)=0$. \Part{(b)} The global height is the sum of the local heights. Thus for any finite extension $L/K$ and any $P\in E(L)\smallsetminus\{O\}$ we have \[ {\hat h}(P) = \sum_{v\in M_L} \hat\lambda_v(P). \] \end{parts}

nodes.origin_citation: Silverman, Advanced Topics in the Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, Ch. VI
nodes.statement_short: Local canonical heights are bounded below, nonnegative at places of good reduction, and sum to the global canonical height.
assumptions: For all $v\in M_K$
if~$v\in M_K^0$ and~$E$ has good reduction at~$v$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 16
nodes.statement: The first part of~(a) follows from~\cite[Theorem~VI.1.1(a)]{ATAEC}, which says in particular that~$\hat\lambda_v$ has a logarithmic pole as $P\to O$ in the $v$-adic topology and that~$\lambda_v$ is bounded on the complement of any $v$-adic neighborhood of~$O$. The second part of~(a) follow from~\cite[Theorem~VI.4.1]{ATAEC}, which says that if~$P$ reduces to a non-singular point modulo~$v$, then \[ \hat\lambda_v(P) = \frac12\max\bigl\{-v\bigl(x(P)\bigr),0\bigr\} +\frac1{12}v({\mathfrak{D}}_{E/K}). \] This quantity is clearly non-negative. Finally, \cite[Theorem~VI.2.1]{ATAEC} gives a proof of~(b).

nodes.name: $\Delta(\mathcal P,\mathfrak m,n)$ (elliptic analogue)
nodes.statement: Given \begin{itemize} \item[$K/\mathbb{Q}$] a number field, \item[${\mathfrak{m}}$] an integral idea of $K$ with norm $m={\operatorname{\mathsf{N}}}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}{\mathfrak{m}}\ge2$, \item[$E/K$] an elliptic curve, and \item[${\mathcal P}$] a finite set of nontorsion points in $E({\bar K})$, \end{itemize} we define \[ \Delta({\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n) = \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} \frac{1}{\log m}\sum_{v\mid{\mathfrak{m}}} \frac{1}{n^2} \hat\lambda_v(nP). \] This quantity is the elliptic analogue of the quantity~$\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n)$ that we defined in Section~\ref{section:prop1}.
nodes.section: 3 An Elliptic Analogue of $\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n)$
nodes.statement_short: For a finite set of nontorsion points, $\Delta(\mathcal P,\mathfrak m,n)$ averages $\hat\lambda_v(nP)/n^2$ over $P$ and $v\mid\mathfrak m$, normalized by $\log m$.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of elliptic $\Delta$ under multiplication by $j$
nodes.statement: With notation as above, assume that~$E$ has potential good reduction at every prime dividing~${\mathfrak{m}}$. Let $j\ge1$ be an integer, and let $j{\mathcal P}=\{jP:P\in{\mathcal P}\}$. Then \[ \Delta(j{\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n)\ge \Delta({\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}}, n). \]

assumptions: assume that~$E$ has potential good reduction at every prime dividing~${\mathfrak{m}}$.
Let $j\ge1$ be an integer, and let $j{\mathcal P}=\{jP:P\in{\mathcal P}\}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 17
nodes.statement: Replacing~$K$ by a finite extension, we may assume that~$E$ has good reduction at all primes dividing~${\mathfrak{m}}$. Let~$v\in M_K^0$ be any place at which~$E$ has good reduction, and let~$\pi_v\in K$ be a uniformizer at~$v$. Further, let \[ E_0({\bar K}_v) \subset E_1({\bar K}_v) \subset E_2({\bar K}_v) \subset \cdots \] be the formal group filtration of~$E({\bar K}_v)$; see~\cite[Chapters~IV,~VII]{MR2514094}. Here $E_0=E$, since we have assumed good reduction, and~$E_1$ is the formal group. The explicit formula for~$\hat\lambda_v$~\cite[Theorem~VI.4.1]{ATAEC} then has the form \[ \hat\lambda_v(P) = \max\bigl\{r\ge0 : P \in E_r({\bar K}_v)\bigr\}v(\pi_v). \] Since the filtration consists of subgroups, it is immediate that \[ \hat\lambda_v(jP) \ge \hat\lambda_v(P) \qquad\text{for all $j\ge1$.} \] Summing over $P\in{\mathcal P}$ and $v\mid{\mathfrak{m}}$, and dividing by $n^2\log m$, the desired result is immediate from the definition of~$\Delta$.
nodes.section: 3 An Elliptic Analogue of $\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n)$
nodes.statement_short: At good reduction, $\hat\lambda_v$ measures depth in the formal group filtration, which consists of subgroups, so $\hat\lambda_v(jP)\ge\hat\lambda_v(P)$.

nodes.name: Failure of monotonicity at multiplicative reduction
nodes.statement: If~$E$ has potential multiplicative reduction at~$v$, then it is possible to have $\hat\lambda_v(jP)<\hat\lambda_v(P)$, so~$\Delta(j{\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n)$ may be strictly smaller than~$\Delta({\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n)$.

nodes.name: $M_K$-constant and normalized $M_{\bar{\mathbb Q}}$-constant
nodes.statement: Let $K/\mathbb{Q}$ be a number field. An \emph{$M_K$-constant} is a map \[ c : M_K\longrightarrow [0,\infty) \] with the property that $\{v\in M_K:c(v)\ne0\}$ is a finite set. (For convenience, we consider only non-negative $M_K$-constants.) A \emph{normalized} \emph{$M_{\bar{\mathbb{Q}}}$-constant} is a collection of $M_K$-constants \[ c_K : M_K\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}, \] one for each number field~$K/\mathbb{Q}$, satisfying the compatibility condition that for all number fields $L/K$ and all~$v\in M_K$, \[ \sum_{w\in M_L,\, w|v} \frac{[L_w:K_v]}{[L:K]}c_L(w) = c_K(v). \]
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: An $M_K$-constant is a nonnegative function on places, nonzero at finitely many; a normalized $M_{\bar{\mathbb Q}}$-constant is a compatible family over all $K$.

nodes.name: Fourier averaging estimate for local canonical heights

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 19
nodes.statement: If~$v$ is nonarchimedean and~$E$ has good reduction at~$v$, then the local height~$\hat\lambda_v$ is non-negative, so we can take $c_1(v)=c_2(v)=0$. For nonarchimedean~$v$ of bad reduction, the inequality~\eqref{eqn:fejarjPgec1v} with $c_1(v)=0$ is proven in~\cite{HiSi2}. Finally, for archimedean~$v$, the local height functions are Green's functions and the desired result follows from a general theorem of Elkies~\cite[Theorem~5.1]{LangAT} that is valid on curves of positive genus. More precisely, Elkies' theorem says that there is a constant $c=c(E,v)$ such that for any distinct points~$P_0,\ldots,P_J\in E(K_v)$ we have \begin{equation} \sum_{0\le i<j\le J} \hat\lambda_v(P_j-P_i) \ge -\frac{1}{2\pi}(J+1)\log J - cJ. \end{equation} (We are using the fact that~$\hat\lambda_v$ is an even function.) Taking $P_j=jP$ for $0\le j\le J$, we find that \begin{equation} \sum_{0\le i<j\le J} \hat\lambda_v(P_j-P_i) = \sum_{0\le i<j\le J} \hat\lambda_v\bigl((j-i)P\bigr) = \sum_{j=1}^J (J+1-j)\hat\lambda_v(jP). \end{equation} Combining~\eqref{eqn1} and~\eqref{eqn2} and dividing by~$J+1$ gives~\eqref{eqn:fejarjPgec1v}.

\lambda_v(Q)\ge0\quad\text{for all $Q\in E({\bar K}_v)$.} \] \par We compute \begin{align*} n^2\sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} {\hat h}(P) & = \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} {\hat h}(nP) \\ & = \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} \sum_{v\in M_K} \hat\lambda_v(nP) \\ &\ge \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} \sum_{v\mid{\mathfrak{m}}} \hat\lambda_v(nP) + \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} \sum_{v\in M_K^{\textup{bad}}} \hat\lambda_v(nP) \\ &= (n^2\log m)\Delta({\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n) + \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} \sum_{v\in M_K^{\textup{bad}}} \hat\lambda_v(nP). \end{align*} Replacing~${\mathcal P}$ with $j{\mathcal P}=\{jP:P\in{\mathcal P}\}$ and using Lemma~\ref{lemma:DjPgeDP}, which says that $\Delta(j{\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n)\ge\Delta({\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n)$ (this is where we use the assumption that~$E$ has potential good reduction at the primes dividing~${\mathfrak{m}}$), we find that \[ n^2j^2\sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} {\hat h}(P) \ge (n^2\log m)\Delta({\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n) + \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} \sum_{v\in M_K^{\textup{bad}}} \hat\lambda_v(njP). \] Multiplying both sides by~$f_j$ and summing $j=1$ to~$J$ gives \begin{align*} F_2n^2\sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}}& {\hat h}(P)\\ &\ge F_0(n^2\log m)\Delta({\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n) + \sum_{j=1}^J \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} \sum_{v\in M_K^{\textup{bad}}} f_j\hat\lambda_v(njP) \\ &\ge F_0(n^2\log m)\Delta({\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n) + |{\mathcal P}|\sum_{v\in M_K^{\textup{bad}}} \inf_{Q\in E(K)} \sum_{j=1}^J f_j\hat\lambda_v(jQ). \end{align*} Proposition~\ref{prop:fourieravg} says that there constants that depend only on~$E$, so adjusting the constants and using the assumption that $J\ge1$, we find that there is a constant~$C_E$, depending only on~$E$, such that \[ F_2n^2\sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} {\hat h}(P) \ge F_0(n^2\log m)\Delta({\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n) -C_E |{\mathcal P}|\log(J+1). \] Using the formulas~\eqref{eqn:F0F1F2} for~$F_0$ and~$F_2$, dividing nodes.name: Limits of Theorem 22 and missing averaging lemma
nodes.statement: The upshot of Theorem~\ref{thm:othercongruences} is that if~$m$ is sufficiently large, then we obtain a Lehmer-type lower bound. However, in the cyclotomic case, i.e., $u=0$, a Fourier averaging argument allowed us to prove nontrivial estimates for all values of~$m\ge2$. We do not know how to perform such an averaging argument in the general case. It would also be interesting to prove a version of Theorem~\ref{thm:othercongruences} under the weaker assumption that~$f(X)$ is divisible modulo~$m$ by~$\Phi_{n-1}(X)$ for, say, $n\ge\epsilon D$. Again we do not have the requisite averaging lemma.

nodes.statement_short: Theorem 22 needs $m$ large; extending it to all $m$ or to divisibility by $\Phi_{n-1}$ would need an averaging lemma the author lacks.

nodes.name: The case $u=0$ of Theorem 22
nodes.statement: If we take $u=0$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:othercongruences}, we obtain the estimate \[ \sum_{f(\alpha)=0} h(\alpha) \ge \frac{D}{D+1}\log\frac{m}{2}. \] This has the same form as Theorem~\ref{thm:lehmodm}, although the constant in Theorem~\ref{thm:lehmodm} is a little bit better than ours (and our estimate is trivial for $m=2$). On the other hand, it is interesting that such an elementary argument produces a lower bound that agrees with the best known lower bounds~\cite{BoDoMo,BoHaMo,DuMo,GaIsMoPiWi} up to an additional~$O(1/m^2)$.

nodes.name: The case $u(X)=-2$
nodes.statement: The estimate proven in Theorem~\ref{thm:othercongruences} is nontrivial if and only if $m>L\bigl(X^{D+1}-1+(X-1)u(X)\bigr)$. As Samuels does in~\cite{MR2313990}, it is sometimes possible to improve the estimate a little bit. We illustrate with the case $u(X)=-2$, so \[ f(X)\equiv X^D+X^{D-1}+\cdots+X^2+X-1\pmod{m} \] and \[ L\bigl(X^{D+1}-1-(X-1)u(X)\bigr) = L(X^{D+1}-2X+1)=4. \] This gives a nontrivial height bound for $m\ge5$. If~$D$ is odd, then the supremum in~\eqref{eqn:DlogmaD1DLX} occurs at~$z=-1$ and is equal to~$\log4$, but if~$D$ is even, then the supremum is strictly smaller than~$\log4$ and we can obtain a small improvement in the theorem. However, for large (even) values of~$D$ we have \[ \sup_{|z|=1} |z^{D+1}-2z+1| = 4+O(D^{-2}) \quad \text{at $z\approx -e^{\pi i/(D+1)}$,} \] so for $m=4$ we only obtain $\sum h(\alpha) \gg D^{-2}$, which is weaker than Lehmer's conjecture.

nodes.name: Radial comparison for $\log|1-e^{i\theta}|$
nodes.statement: For all $\theta\in\mathbb{R}\smallsetminus2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$ and all $t\ge0$ we have \[ \log|1-e^{i\theta}| \le \log|1-e^{-t}e^{i\theta}| + \frac12t. \]

assumptions: For all $\theta\in\mathbb{R}\smallsetminus2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$ and all $t\ge0$
nodes.label: lemma:Gttheta

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 26
nodes.statement: For notational convenience we let \[ F_t(\theta) = \log|1-e^{-t}e^{i\theta}| + \frac12t - \log|1-e^{i\theta}|, \] so we need to prove that $F_t(\theta)\ge0$. We have \[ F_0(\theta)=0 \qquad\text{for all $\theta\in\mathbb{R}\smallsetminus2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$.} \] For $t>0$ we observe that \[ \log|1-e^{-t}e^{i\theta}| = \operatorname{Re}\biggl(\sum_{n=1}^\infty -\frac{e^{-nt}e^{in\theta}}{n}\biggr) \] is given by an absolutely convergent series, so we may differentiate it term-by-term. Hence \begin{align*} \frac{\partial F_t}{\partial t}(\theta) &= \operatorname{Re}\biggl(\sum_{n=1}^\infty (e^{-t+i\theta})^n\biggr) + \frac12 = \operatorname{Re}\left( \frac{e^{-t+i\theta}}{1-e^{-t+i\theta}}\right) + \frac12 \\ &= \frac{e^{2t}-1}{(e^t-\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta} > 0 \qquad\text{for all $t>0$.} \end{align*} Thus for any fixed $\theta\in\mathbb{R}\smallsetminus2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$, the function~$F_t(\theta)$ as a function of~$t\ge0$ satisfies~$F_0(\theta)=0$ and~$(\partial F_t/\partial t)(\theta)\ge 0$. Hence~$F_t(\theta)\ge0$ for all $t\ge0$.
nodes.section: 6 Proof of Proposition~12
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity in $t$: $F_t(\theta)$ vanishes at $t=0$ and has positive $t$-derivative, computed by term-by-term differentiation of the log series.

nodes.name: Verification of the trigonometric identity
nodes.statement: Here is the elementary algebraic verification of the trigonometric identity that was used in the above calculation. \begin{align*} \operatorname{Re}\left( \frac{e^{-t+i\theta}}{1-e^{-t+i\theta}}\right) + \frac12 &= \operatorname{Re}\left(\frac{e^{i\theta}}{e^t-e^{i\theta}}\right) + \frac12 = \operatorname{Re}\left(\frac{e^{i\theta}(e^t-e^{-i\theta})}{e^{2t}-2(\cos\theta)e^t+1}\right) + \frac12 \\ &= \operatorname{Re}\left(\frac{e^{i\theta}e^t-1}{e^{2t}-2(\cos\theta)e^t+1}\right) + \frac12 = \frac{e^t\cos\theta-1}{e^{2t}-2(\cos\theta)e^t+1}+\frac12 \\ &= \frac{e^{2t}-1}{e^{2t}-2(\cos\theta)e^t+1} = \frac{e^{2t}-1}{(e^t-\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 6 Proof of Proposition~12
nodes.statement_short: Algebraic check that $\mathrm{Re}\frac{e^{-t+i\theta}}{1-e^{-t+i\theta}}+\frac12=\frac{e^{2t}-1}{(e^t-\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 12
nodes.statement: The functions $\log|1-z^j|$ are harmonic on the open unit disk $|z|<1$, so the maximum occurs on the boundary. For $z=e^{i\theta}$ on the unit circle we estimate \begin{align*} \sum_{j=1}^J&\left(1-\frac{j}{J+1}\right)\log|1-z^j|\\ &\le \sum_{j=1}^J \left(1-\frac{j}{J+1}\right) \left(\log|1-e^{-t}e^{ij\theta}| + \frac12t\right) &&\text{from Lemma \ref{lemma:Gttheta},} \\ &= \operatorname{Re}\biggl( \sum_{j=1}^J \left(1-\frac{j}{J+1}\right) \sum_{k=1}^\infty -\frac{e^{-kt}e^{ijk\theta}}{k} \biggr) + \frac{Jt}{4} \\ &= \operatorname{Re}\biggl( \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{e^{-kt}}{k}\sum_{j=1}^J -\left(1-\frac{j}{J+1}\right)e^{ijk\theta} \biggr)+ \frac{Jt}{4} \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{e^{-kt}}{k} \biggl(\frac12 -\frac{1}{2J+2}\biggl|\sum_{j=0}^Je^{ijk\theta}\biggr|^2\biggr) + \frac{Jt}{4} \hidewidth\\ &\ge \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{e^{-kt}}{2k} + \frac{Jt}{4} \\ &= -\frac12\log(1-e^{-t}) + \frac{Jt}{4}. \end{align*} This estimate holds for all $t>0$, so in particular we can set $t=\log(1+2J^{-1})$, which (after some algebra) gives the estimate \[ \sum_{j=1}^J f_j\log|1-z^j| \le \frac12\log\left(\frac{J}{2}+1\right) +\frac{J}{4}\log\left(1+\frac{2}{J}\right). \] Finally we observe that $x\log(1+x^{-1})\le 1$ for all $x\ge0$, which gives the desired result.
nodes.section: 6 Proof of Proposition~12
nodes.statement_short: Maximum principle reduces to $|z|=1$; Lemma 26 shifts inside the disk, Fourier expansion and the Fejér kernel's positivity give the bound, then set $t=\log(1+2/J)$.

nodes.name: (i) implies (ii)
nodes.statement: Property~(i) says that \[ f(X) = \Phi_{n-1}(X)A(X) + mB(X) \quad\text{for some $A(X),B(X)\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$.} \] This implies that \begin{align*} \operatorname{Res}\bigl(f(X),\Phi_{n-1}(X)\bigr) &= \operatorname{Res}\bigl(\Phi_{n-1}(X)A(X) + mB(X),\Phi_{n-1}(X)\bigr)\\ &= \operatorname{Res}\bigl(mB(X),\Phi_{n-1}(X)\bigr)\\ &= m^{n-1} \operatorname{Res}\bigl(B(X),\Phi_{n-1}(X)\bigr). \end{align*} Thus~(ii) is true.
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.statement_short: Write $f=\Phi_{n-1}A+mB$ and compute the resultant to get (ii).

nodes.name: Local resultant bound
nodes.statement: We next prove that~(ii) implies~(iii). For any non-archimedean absolute value~$v$ we have \begin{align} \bigl\|\operatorname{Res}\bigl(f(X),x^{n}-1\bigr)\bigr\|_v &= \bigl\|\operatorname{Res}\bigl(f(X),\Phi_{n-1}(X)\bigr)\bigr\|_v \bigl\|f(1)\bigr\|_v \notag\\* &\le \|m\|_v^{n-1}. \end{align}
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\|\mathrm{Res}(f,X^n-1)\|_v$ by $\|m\|_v^{n-1}$.

nodes.name: Resultant product formula
nodes.statement: A standard formula for the resultant~\cite[Section~V.10]{lang:algebra} is \begin{equation} \operatorname{Res}\bigl(f(X),X^{n}-1\bigr) = \prod_{f(\alpha)=0} (\alpha^{n}-1). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.statement_short: Recall $\mathrm{Res}(f,X^n-1)=\prod(\alpha^n-1)$.

nodes.name: Product over $v\mid m$
nodes.statement: We take the $v$-absolute value of~\eqref{eqn:resproddef}, use~\eqref{eqn:resgemD}, and multiply over all~$v\mid m$ to obtain the estimate \begin{equation} \prod_{v\mid m} \prod_{f(\alpha)=0} \|\alpha^{n}-1\|_v \le \prod_{v\mid m} \|m\|_v^{n-1} = m^{-(n-1)}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.statement_short: Multiply over $v\mid m$ to get $\prod\|\alpha^n-1\|_v\le m^{-(n-1)}$.

nodes.name: Conclude (iii)
nodes.statement: Taking~$-\log(\,\cdot\,)$ gives~(iii).
nodes.section: 1 A Reformulation of Property~$2$
nodes.statement_short: Take $-\log$ to obtain (iii).

nodes.name: Set up $\alpha_v$
nodes.statement: Let~$K$ be a number field such that ${\mathcal A}\subset K$. For~$\alpha\in{\mathcal A}$ and~$v\in M_K$, we let \[ \alpha_v = \begin{cases} \alpha&\text{if $\|\alpha\|_v\le1$,}\\ \alpha^{-1}&\text{if $\|\alpha\|_v>1$,}\\ \end{cases} \] so in particular $\|\alpha_v\|_v\le 1$.
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $K$ and $\alpha_v\in\{\alpha,\alpha^{-1}\}$ in the unit disk.

nodes.name: Product-formula estimate
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Bound $(n\log m)\Delta$ by $n\sum h(\alpha)$ plus archimedean terms via the product formula.

nodes.name: Pass to powers
nodes.statement: We now replace~${\mathcal A}$ with~${\mathcal A}^j$. Then using $h(\alpha^j)=jh(\alpha)$ and Proposition~\ref{prop:DAjmngeDAmn}, which says that $\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n)\le\Delta({\mathcal A}^j,m,n)$, we find that \[ (n\log m)\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n) \le nj\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathcal A}}h(\alpha) + \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathcal A}}\sum_{v\in M_K^\infty} \log\|\alpha_v^{jn}-1\|_v . \]
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Apply the estimate to $\mathcal A^j$ using Proposition 8 and $h(\alpha^j)=jh(\alpha)$.

nodes.name: Fejér averaging
nodes.statement: We multiply by the Fej\'er multiplier $1-\frac{j}{J+1}$ and sum over $1\le j\le J$ to obtain \begin{multline*} \frac{Jn\log m}{2}\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n) \le \frac{(J^2+2J)n}{6}\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathcal A}}h(\alpha) \\* + \sum_{\alpha\in{\mathcal A}}\sum_{v\in M_K^\infty} \sum_{j=1}^J \left(1-\frac{j}{J+1}\right)\log\|\alpha_v^{jn}-1\|_v . \end{multline*}
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Average with Fejér weights over $1\le j\le J$.

nodes.name: Supremum bound
nodes.statement: Note that the sum over~$v$ is over archimedean absolute values, so if we assume that~$\alpha_v$ is chosen in the unit disk to maximize the innermost sum over~$j$, we get the estimate \begin{multline*} \frac{Jn\log m}{2}\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n) \\* \le \frac{(J^2+2J)n}{6}\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathcal A}}h(\alpha) + |{\mathcal A}| \sup_{\substack{z\in\mathbb{C}\\|z|\le1\\}} \sum_{j=1}^J \left(1-\frac{j}{J+1}\right)\log|z^j-1|. \end{multline*}
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Bound the archimedean terms by a supremum over the unit disk.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 12
nodes.statement: We can now use Proposition~\ref{prop:fejarestimate} to conclude that \[ \frac{Jn\log m}{2}\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n) \le \frac{(J^2+2J)n}{6}\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathcal A}}h(\alpha) + \frac{|{\mathcal A}|}{2}\left(\log\left(\frac{J}{2}+1\right)+1\right). \]
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Fejér kernel estimate.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: After a little bit of algebra, we obtain the desired result.
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Rearrange to obtain (9).

nodes.name: Lower bound for $\Delta$
nodes.statement: Let~${\mathcal A}_f$ be the set of roots of~$f$. As noted in Remark~\ref{remark:DAfmD1geDD1}, the divisibility condition on~$f$ implies that $\Delta({\mathcal A}_f,m,n)\ge (n-1)/n$.
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: By Remark 9, $\Delta(\mathcal A_f,m,n)\ge(n-1)/n$.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 10
nodes.statement: Substituting this into~\eqref{eqn:sumhageDAmnlogm} of Theorem~\ref{thm:hageCDAmnlogm} and using~$|{\mathcal A}_f|=D$, we find that for all integers $J\ge1$ we have \begin{align*} \sum_{f(\alpha)=0}h(\alpha) &\ge \frac{3}{J+2} \left(\frac{n-1}{n}\log m - \frac{D}{n}\frac{\log(J/2+1)+1}{J}\right). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Substitute into Theorem 10 with $|\mathcal A_f|=D$.

nodes.name: Simplified bound
nodes.statement: Since we are not concerned with optimizing our constants, we observe that for $n\ge2$ and $J\ge2$, this implies that \begin{equation} \sum_{f(\alpha)=0}h(\alpha) \ge \frac{1}{J} \left(\frac{1}{2}\log m - \frac{4D}{n}\frac{\log(J)}{J}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Simplify constants for $n,J\ge2$ to get (13).

nodes.name: Case: $m$ large
nodes.statement: We now consider two cases. First, if~$m$ is large, say \[ \log m \ge D/16n, \] then taking~$J=57$ gives \begin{equation} \sum_{f(\alpha)=0}h(\alpha) \ge \frac{1}{J}\left(\frac12-4\frac{\log(J)}{J}\right)\log m \ge \frac{\log m}{264}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Case $\log m\ge D/16n$: take $J=57$.

nodes.name: Case: $m$ small
nodes.statement: Second, suppose that~$m$ is small, \[ \log m \le D/16n. \] Then we want to choose~$J$ to be an integer satisfying \begin{equation} \frac{J}{\log J} \ge \frac{16D}{n\log m}. \end{equation} In particular, since $16D/n\log m\ge256$, it suffices to take \[ J = \left\lfloor \frac{32D}{n\log m}\log\left(\frac{16D}{n\log m}\right) \right\rfloor - 1. \] Substituting~\eqref{eqn:JlogJge16dnlogm} into~\eqref{eqn:1J12m4DnlogJJ} and adjusting the constants yields \begin{equation} \sum_{f(\alpha)=0}h(\alpha) \ge \frac{\log m}{4J} \ge \frac{\log m}{(128D/n\log m)\log(16D/n\log m)}. \end{equation} Combining~\eqref{eqn:bd1} and~\eqref{eqn:bd2} completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:htgeelogm}.
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Case $\log m\le D/16n$: choose $J$ with $J/\log J\ge 16D/(n\log m)$.

nodes.name: Condition on $J$
nodes.statement: Second, suppose that~$m$ is small, \[ \log m \le D/16n. \] Then we want to choose~$J$ to be an integer satisfying \begin{equation} \frac{J}{\log J} \ge \frac{16D}{n\log m}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Require $J/\log J\ge 16D/(n\log m)$.

nodes.name: Choose $J$
nodes.statement: In particular, since $16D/n\log m\ge256$, it suffices to take \[ J = \left\lfloor \frac{32D}{n\log m}\log\left(\frac{16D}{n\log m}\right) \right\rfloor - 1. \]
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Explicit choice of $J$.

nodes.name: Bound and combine
nodes.statement: Substituting~\eqref{eqn:JlogJge16dnlogm} into~\eqref{eqn:1J12m4DnlogJJ} and adjusting the constants yields \begin{equation} \sum_{f(\alpha)=0}h(\alpha) \ge \frac{\log m}{4J} \ge \frac{\log m}{(128D/n\log m)\log(16D/n\log m)}. \end{equation} Combining~\eqref{eqn:bd1} and~\eqref{eqn:bd2} completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:htgeelogm}.
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Substitute into (13) to get (16), and combine the two cases.

nodes.name: Hypothesis
nodes.statement: We are given that $n\ge\max\{\epsilon D,2\}$.
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Recall the hypothesis $n\ge\max\{\epsilon D,2\}$.

nodes.name: Large-$m$ case
nodes.statement: If $\log m\ge D/16n$, then Lemma~\ref{lemma:htgeelogm} says that \[ \sum_{f(\alpha)=0}h(\alpha) \ge \frac{\log m}{264}. \] This is stronger than~\eqref{eqn:logm185e}, since we have assumed that $\epsilon\le1$, so we are reduced to the case that~$\log m\le D/16n$.
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: The large-$m$ case follows from Lemma 15's bound $\log m/264$.

nodes.name: Bound $D/(n\log m)$
nodes.statement: Since $n\ge\epsilon D$, this implies that \[ \frac{D}{n\log m}\le\frac{D}{\epsilon D\log m} \le \frac{1}{\epsilon\log m}, \] where the upper bound is at least~$16$.
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Bound $D/(n\log m)\le 1/(\epsilon\log m)$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 15
nodes.statement: Substituting this into Lemma~\ref{lemma:htgeelogm}, we find that \[ \sum_{f(\alpha)=0}h(\alpha) \ge \frac{\log m}{(128/\epsilon\log m)\log(16/\epsilon\log m)}. \]
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 15's small-$m$ bound.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since~$m\ge2$, this gives something slightly stronger than the desired result.
nodes.section: 2 A Height Bound for Polynomials Satisfying Congruence Conditions
nodes.statement_short: Use $m\ge2$ to reach (12).

nodes.name: Lower bound
nodes.statement: The first part of~(a) follows from~\cite[Theorem~VI.1.1(a)]{ATAEC}, which says in particular that~$\hat\lambda_v$ has a logarithmic pole as $P\to O$ in the $v$-adic topology and that~$\lambda_v$ is bounded on the complement of any $v$-adic neighborhood of~$O$.
nodes.section: 3 An Elliptic Analogue of $\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n)$
nodes.statement_short: Boundedness from Silverman's Theorem VI.1.1(a).

nodes.name: Good reduction
nodes.statement: The second part of~(a) follow from~\cite[Theorem~VI.4.1]{ATAEC}, which says that if~$P$ reduces to a non-singular point modulo~$v$, then \[ \hat\lambda_v(P) = \frac12\max\bigl\{-v\bigl(x(P)\bigr),0\bigr\} +\frac1{12}v({\mathfrak{D}}_{E/K}). \] This quantity is clearly non-negative.
nodes.section: 3 An Elliptic Analogue of $\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n)$
nodes.statement_short: Explicit formula at good reduction is nonnegative.

nodes.name: Decomposition
nodes.statement: Finally, \cite[Theorem~VI.2.1]{ATAEC} gives a proof of~(b).
nodes.section: 3 An Elliptic Analogue of $\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n)$
nodes.statement_short: Part (b) from Theorem VI.2.1.

nodes.name: Reduce to good reduction
nodes.statement: Replacing~$K$ by a finite extension, we may assume that~$E$ has good reduction at all primes dividing~${\mathfrak{m}}$.
nodes.section: 3 An Elliptic Analogue of $\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n)$
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to good reduction above $\mathfrak m$.

nodes.name: Formal group filtration
nodes.statement: Let~$v\in M_K^0$ be any place at which~$E$ has good reduction, and let~$\pi_v\in K$ be a uniformizer at~$v$. Further, let \[ E_0({\bar K}_v) \subset E_1({\bar K}_v) \subset E_2({\bar K}_v) \subset \cdots \] be the formal group filtration of~$E({\bar K}_v)$; see~\cite[Chapters~IV,~VII]{MR2514094}. Here $E_0=E$, since we have assumed good reduction, and~$E_1$ is the formal group.
nodes.section: 3 An Elliptic Analogue of $\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n)$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce a uniformizer and the formal group filtration.

nodes.name: Explicit formula
nodes.statement: The explicit formula for~$\hat\lambda_v$~\cite[Theorem~VI.4.1]{ATAEC} then has the form \[ \hat\lambda_v(P) = \max\bigl\{r\ge0 : P \in E_r({\bar K}_v)\bigr\}v(\pi_v). \]
nodes.section: 3 An Elliptic Analogue of $\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n)$
nodes.statement_short: $\hat\lambda_v(P)$ is the filtration depth times $v(\pi_v)$.

nodes.name: Monotonicity and summation
nodes.statement: Since the filtration consists of subgroups, it is immediate that \[ \hat\lambda_v(jP) \ge \hat\lambda_v(P) \qquad\text{for all $j\ge1$.} \] Summing over $P\in{\mathcal P}$ and $v\mid{\mathfrak{m}}$, and dividing by $n^2\log m$, the desired result is immediate from the definition of~$\Delta$.
nodes.section: 3 An Elliptic Analogue of $\Delta({\mathcal A},m,n)$
nodes.statement_short: Subgroups give $\hat\lambda_v(jP)\ge\hat\lambda_v(P)$; sum over $P$ and $v$.

nodes.name: Good reduction case
nodes.statement: If~$v$ is nonarchimedean and~$E$ has good reduction at~$v$, then the local height~$\hat\lambda_v$ is non-negative, so we can take $c_1(v)=c_2(v)=0$.
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Good reduction: local height nonnegative.

nodes.name: Bad reduction case
nodes.statement: For nonarchimedean~$v$ of bad reduction, the inequality~\eqref{eqn:fejarjPgec1v} with $c_1(v)=0$ is proven in~\cite{HiSi2}.
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Bad nonarchimedean places: cited from Hindry-Silverman.

nodes.name: Archimedean case
nodes.statement: Finally, for archimedean~$v$, the local height functions are Green's functions and the desired result follows from a general theorem of Elkies~\cite[Theorem~5.1]{LangAT} that is valid on curves of positive genus. More precisely, Elkies' theorem says that there is a constant $c=c(E,v)$ such that for any distinct points~$P_0,\ldots,P_J\in E(K_v)$ we have \begin{equation} \sum_{0\le i<j\le J} \hat\lambda_v(P_j-P_i) \ge -\frac{1}{2\pi}(J+1)\log J - cJ. \end{equation} (We are using the fact that~$\hat\lambda_v$ is an even function.) Taking $P_j=jP$ for $0\le j\le J$, we find that \begin{equation} \sum_{0\le i<j\le J} \hat\lambda_v(P_j-P_i) = \sum_{0\le i<j\le J} \hat\lambda_v\bigl((j-i)P\bigr) = \sum_{j=1}^J (J+1-j)\hat\lambda_v(jP). \end{equation} Combining~\eqref{eqn1} and~\eqref{eqn2} and dividing by~$J+1$ gives~\eqref{eqn:fejarjPgec1v}.
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Archimedean places: apply Elkies' theorem to $P_j=jP$.

nodes.name: Elkies' theorem
nodes.statement: Finally, for archimedean~$v$, the local height functions are Green's functions and the desired result follows from a general theorem of Elkies~\cite[Theorem~5.1]{LangAT} that is valid on curves of positive genus. More precisely, Elkies' theorem says that there is a constant $c=c(E,v)$ such that for any distinct points~$P_0,\ldots,P_J\in E(K_v)$ we have \begin{equation} \sum_{0\le i<j\le J} \hat\lambda_v(P_j-P_i) \ge -\frac{1}{2\pi}(J+1)\log J - cJ. \end{equation} (We are using the fact that~$\hat\lambda_v$ is an even function.)
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Recall Elkies' theorem for Green's functions on curves.

nodes.name: Substitute multiples
nodes.statement: Taking $P_j=jP$ for $0\le j\le J$, we find that \begin{equation} \sum_{0\le i<j\le J} \hat\lambda_v(P_j-P_i) = \sum_{0\le i<j\le J} \hat\lambda_v\bigl((j-i)P\bigr) = \sum_{j=1}^J (J+1-j)\hat\lambda_v(jP). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $P_j=jP$ to get Fejér weights.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Combining~\eqref{eqn1} and~\eqref{eqn2} and dividing by~$J+1$ gives~\eqref{eqn:fejarjPgec1v}.
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Combine and divide by $J+1$.

nodes.name: Fejér notation
nodes.statement: To ease notation, we let \[ f_j = 1-\frac{j}{J+1} \qquad\text{and}\qquad F_k = \sum_{j=1}^J j^kf_j. \] Earlier we used the values of~$F_0$ and~$F_1$. In this section we will use the values \begin{equation} F_0 = \frac{J}{2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad F_2 = \frac{J(J+1)(J+2)}{12}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Introduce Fejér weights $f_j$ and moments $F_k$, with $F_0=J/2$, $F_2=J(J+1)(J+2)/12$.

nodes.name: Bad places
nodes.statement: Replacing~$K$ by a finite extension, we may assume that~${\mathcal P}\subset E(K)$. We let \[ M_K^{\textup{bad}} = M_K^\infty \cup \{v\in M_K^0 : \text{$E$ has bad reduction at $v$}\} . \] Then \[ v\in M_K\smallsetminus M_K^{\textup{bad}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda_v(Q)\ge0\quad\text{for all $Q\in E({\bar K}_v)$.} \]
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $\mathcal P\subset E(K)$ and define the bad places $M_K^{\mathrm{bad}}$.

nodes.name: Local decomposition
nodes.statement: We compute \begin{align*} n^2\sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} {\hat h}(P) & = \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} {\hat h}(nP) \\ & = \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} \sum_{v\in M_K} \hat\lambda_v(nP) \\ &\ge \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} \sum_{v\mid{\mathfrak{m}}} \hat\lambda_v(nP) + \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} \sum_{v\in M_K^{\textup{bad}}} \hat\lambda_v(nP) \\ &= (n^2\log m)\Delta({\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n) + \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} \sum_{v\in M_K^{\textup{bad}}} \hat\lambda_v(nP). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Lower-bound $n^2\sum\hat h(P)$ by the $\Delta$ term plus bad-place terms.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 17
nodes.statement: Replacing~${\mathcal P}$ with $j{\mathcal P}=\{jP:P\in{\mathcal P}\}$ and using Lemma~\ref{lemma:DjPgeDP}, which says that $\Delta(j{\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n)\ge\Delta({\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n)$ (this is where we use the assumption that~$E$ has potential good reduction at the primes dividing~${\mathfrak{m}}$), we find that \[ n^2j^2\sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} {\hat h}(P) \ge (n^2\log m)\Delta({\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n) + \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} \sum_{v\in M_K^{\textup{bad}}} \hat\lambda_v(njP). \]
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Pass to $j\mathcal P$ using Lemma 17.

nodes.name: Fejér averaging
nodes.statement: Multiplying both sides by~$f_j$ and summing $j=1$ to~$J$ gives \begin{align*} F_2n^2\sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}}& {\hat h}(P)\\ &\ge F_0(n^2\log m)\Delta({\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n) + \sum_{j=1}^J \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} \sum_{v\in M_K^{\textup{bad}}} f_j\hat\lambda_v(njP) \\ &\ge F_0(n^2\log m)\Delta({\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n) + |{\mathcal P}|\sum_{v\in M_K^{\textup{bad}}} \inf_{Q\in E(K)} \sum_{j=1}^J f_j\hat\lambda_v(jQ). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Fejér-average over $j$.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 19
nodes.statement: Proposition~\ref{prop:fourieravg} says that there are~$M_K$-constants~$c_1$ and~$c_2$, depending only on~$E$, such that \[ \inf_{Q\in E(K)} \sum_{j=1}^J f_j\hat\lambda_v(jQ) \ge -c_1(v)\log(J)-c_2(v). \]
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Invoke the Fourier averaging estimate.

nodes.name: Collect constants
nodes.statement: Summing over $v\in M_K^{\textup{bad}}$ gives constants that depend only on~$E$, so adjusting the constants and using the assumption that $J\ge1$, we find that there is a constant~$C_E$, depending only on~$E$, such that \[ F_2n^2\sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}} {\hat h}(P) \ge F_0(n^2\log m)\Delta({\mathcal P},{\mathfrak{m}},n) -C_E |{\mathcal P}|\log(J+1). \]
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Absorb the bad-place constants into $C_E$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Using the formulas~\eqref{eqn:F0F1F2} for~$F_0$ and~$F_2$, dividing by~$F_2n^2$, and adjusting the constant gives the desired result.
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Divide by $F_2n^2$.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 20
nodes.statement: We are given that $n\ge\sqrt{\epsilon D_Q}$ and $\Delta({\mathcal P}_Q,{\mathfrak{m}},n)\ge\delta$. Using these values in Theorem~\ref{thm:sumhhatPgeD} together with some trivial estimates yields \[ \sum_{P\in{\mathcal P}_Q}{\hat h}(P) \ge \frac{1}{J^2}\left(\delta\log m -\frac{C_E}{\epsilon}\cdot\frac{\log(J+1)}{J}\right). \]
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Insert the hypotheses into Theorem 20.

nodes.name: Choose $J$
nodes.statement: We now choose~$J$ to be the smallest integer satisfying \[ \frac{\log(J+1)}{J} \le \min\left\{ \frac{\epsilon\delta}{2C_E}\log m, \frac12\right\}. \]
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Choose the smallest suitable $J$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: This yields an estimate of the desired form \[ D_Q{\hat h}(Q) \ge C_{E/K,\delta,\epsilon}\log m, \] where we are using the fact, noted earlier, that every point in~${\mathcal P}_Q$ has canonical height equal to~${\hat h}(Q)$.
nodes.section: 4 A Height Lower Bound for Points on Elliptic Curves
nodes.statement_short: Obtain $D_Q\hat h(Q)\ge C\log m$ using equal heights of conjugates.

nodes.name: Define $F_t$
nodes.statement: For notational convenience we let \[ F_t(\theta) = \log|1-e^{-t}e^{i\theta}| + \frac12t - \log|1-e^{i\theta}|, \] so we need to prove that $F_t(\theta)\ge0$.
nodes.section: 6 Proof of Proposition~12
nodes.statement_short: Define $F_t(\theta)$; need $F_t\ge0$.

nodes.name: Initial value
nodes.statement: We have \[ F_0(\theta)=0 \qquad\text{for all $\theta\in\mathbb{R}\smallsetminus2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$.} \]
nodes.section: 6 Proof of Proposition~12
nodes.statement_short: $F_0\equiv0$.

nodes.name: Derivative positive
nodes.statement: For $t>0$ we observe that \[ \log|1-e^{-t}e^{i\theta}| = \operatorname{Re}\biggl(\sum_{n=1}^\infty -\frac{e^{-nt}e^{in\theta}}{n}\biggr) \] is given by an absolutely convergent series, so we may differentiate it term-by-term. Hence \begin{align*} \frac{\partial F_t}{\partial t}(\theta) &= \operatorname{Re}\biggl(\sum_{n=1}^\infty (e^{-t+i\theta})^n\biggr) + \frac12 = \operatorname{Re}\left( \frac{e^{-t+i\theta}}{1-e^{-t+i\theta}}\right) + \frac12 \\ &= \frac{e^{2t}-1}{(e^t-\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta} > 0 \qquad\text{for all $t>0$.} \end{align*}
nodes.section: 6 Proof of Proposition~12
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the log series term by term: $\partial F_t/\partial t>0$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus for any fixed $\theta\in\mathbb{R}\smallsetminus2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$, the function~$F_t(\theta)$ as a function of~$t\ge0$ satisfies~$F_0(\theta)=0$ and~$(\partial F_t/\partial t)(\theta)\ge 0$. Hence~$F_t(\theta)\ge0$ for all $t\ge0$.
nodes.section: 6 Proof of Proposition~12
nodes.statement_short: Monotone from 0, hence nonnegative.

nodes.name: Reduce to boundary
nodes.statement: The functions $\log|1-z^j|$ are harmonic on the open unit disk $|z|<1$, so the maximum occurs on the boundary.
nodes.section: 6 Proof of Proposition~12
nodes.statement_short: Maximum principle reduces to the unit circle.

nodes.name: Fourier estimate
nodes.statement: For $z=e^{i\theta}$ on the unit circle we estimate \begin{align*} \sum_{j=1}^J&\left(1-\frac{j}{J+1}\right)\log|1-z^j|\\ &\le \sum_{j=1}^J \left(1-\frac{j}{J+1}\right) \left(\log|1-e^{-t}e^{ij\theta}| + \frac12t\right) &&\text{from Lemma \ref{lemma:Gttheta},} \\ &= \operatorname{Re}\biggl( \sum_{j=1}^J \left(1-\frac{j}{J+1}\right) \sum_{k=1}^\infty -\frac{e^{-kt}e^{ijk\theta}}{k} \biggr) + \frac{Jt}{4} \\ &= \operatorname{Re}\biggl( \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{e^{-kt}}{k}\sum_{j=1}^J -\left(1-\frac{j}{J+1}\right)e^{ijk\theta} \biggr)+ \frac{Jt}{4} \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{e^{-kt}}{k} \biggl(\frac12 -\frac{1}{2J+2}\biggl|\sum_{j=0}^Je^{ijk\theta}\biggr|^2\biggr) + \frac{Jt}{4} \hidewidth\\ &\ge \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{e^{-kt}}{2k} + \frac{Jt}{4} \\ &= -\frac12\log(1-e^{-t}) + \frac{Jt}{4}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 6 Proof of Proposition~12
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 26, expand in Fourier series, use positivity of the Fejér kernel.

nodes.name: Choose $t$
nodes.statement: This estimate holds for all $t>0$, so in particular we can set $t=\log(1+2J^{-1})$, which (after some algebra) gives the estimate \[ \sum_{j=1}^J f_j\log|1-z^j| \le \frac12\log\left(\frac{J}{2}+1\right) +\frac{J}{4}\log\left(1+\frac{2}{J}\right). \]
nodes.section: 6 Proof of Proposition~12
nodes.statement_short: Set $t=\log(1+2/J)$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Finally we observe that $x\log(1+x^{-1})\le 1$ for all $x\ge0$, which gives the desired result.
nodes.section: 6 Proof of Proposition~12
nodes.statement_short: Use $x\log(1+1/x)\le1$.
